passages.text: Machine Learning Approach to Predict In‐Hospital Mortality in Patients Admitted for Peripheral Artery Disease in the United States
Background

Peripheral artery disease (PAD) affects >10 million people in the United States. PAD is associated with poor outcomes, including premature death. Machine learning (ML) has been increasingly used on big data to predict clinical outcomes. This study aims to develop ML models to predict in‐hospital mortality in patients hospitalized for PAD based on a national database.
Methods and Results

Inpatient hospitalization data were obtained from the 2016 to 2019 National Inpatient Sample. A total of 150 921 inpatients were identified with a primary diagnosis of PAD and PAD‐related procedures using codes of the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD‐10‐CM) and International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Procedure Coding System (ICD‐10‐PCS). Four ML models, including logistic regression, random forest, light gradient boosting, and extreme gradient boosting models, were trained to predict the risk of in‐hospital death based on a selection of variables, including patient characteristics, comorbidities, procedures, and hospital‐related factors. In‐hospital mortality occurred in 1.8% of patients. The performance of the 4 models was comparable, with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranging from 0.83 to 0.85, sensitivity of 77% to 82%, and specificity of 72% to 75%. These results suggest adequate predictability for clinical decision‐making. In all 4 models, the total number of diagnoses and procedures, age, endovascular revascularization procedure, congestive heart failure, diabetes, and diabetes with complications were critical predictors of in‐hospital mortality.
Conclusions

This study demonstrates the feasibility of ML in predicting in‐hospital mortality in patients with a primary PAD diagnosis. Findings highlight the potential of ML models in identifying high‐risk patients for poor outcomes and guiding personalized intervention.

Clinical Perspective
What Is New?
Assessing the risk of in‐hospital mortality in patients with peripheral artery disease is essential for patient stratification and improving clinical outcomes.

State‐of‐the‐art machine learning models were developed to predict the risk of in‐hospital mortality in patients primarily admitted for peripheral artery disease, based on the 2016 to 2019 National Inpatient Sample database containing >150 000 samples.

The models demonstrated adequate sensitivity and accuracy and suggested that patients who were older, had diabetes, diabetes complications, congestive heart failure, underwent revascularization procedure or multiple procedures, and had multiple diagnoses during hospitalization were at higher risk of dying in the hospital.
What Are the Clinical Implications?
This work lends support to the notion of using machine learning for developing accurate and generalizable risk assessment tools in clinical practice.
These validated models could lead to better management of high‐risk patients and lower mortality, thereby promoting precision medicine in peripheral artery disease.

Peripheral artery disease (PAD) affects 202 million people worldwide, including >10 million in the United States. More than 50% of patients with PAD are asymptomatic and are at an increased risk of heart failure and other vascular diseases. Common risk factors for PAD include smoking, obesity, and diabetes. PAD prevalence in the United States is 2 to 3 times higher in Black patients over age 65, people with diabetes, and current smokers.

People with PAD have an increased risk of mortality compared with people without PAD. With an increasing number of patients with PAD admitted to the hospital, there is an urgent need to optimize treatment to improve clinical outcomes and reduce mortality for patients with PAD. The in‐hospital mortality in the United States among patients hospitalized with PAD was reported as being from 2.5% to 3.1% in the literature, which was similar to in‐hospital mortality for patients with acute ischemic stroke (2.3% to 4.2%) and slightly lower than that among patients with an acute myocardial infarction (4.6%). Studies have reported that patients hospitalized for PAD with anemia, chronic kidney disease, atrial fibrillation, and patients who underwent major lower extremity amputation had higher risk for in‐hospital mortality. However, there is lack of a multifactor model for predicting in‐hospital mortality in patients with PAD, and it remains unclear what risk factors are crucial for this clinical outcome.

Machine learning (ML) has recently been used as a novel approach in data‐driven research to predict clinical outcomes. Compared with traditional regression‐based approaches, ML models can better reveal nonlinear interactions based on historical data. Numerous studies have shown that tree‐based ML models such as random forest and boosting algorithms outperformed regularized logistic regression models, but some reported similar performance between these 2 approaches in certain tasks. Therefore, efforts were made in the current study to address the following research gaps: (1) development of prediction models based on a national database to identify patients hospitalized for PAD who are at increased risk of mortality during hospitalization; and (2) evaluation of different ML algorithms on their performance and feasibility for this task.
Methods
Data Source

All data used in this study are available through the online Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project Central Distributor to any researcher who submits an application and purchases to download the Nationwide data. All models and codes used in the analysis are also accessible from an online repository. Inpatient hospitalization data were obtained from the 2016 to 2019 National Inpatient Sample (NIS). The NIS database was developed for the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality and is the largest nationwide inpatient health care database in the United States. It contains information on patients' demographic characteristics, discharge status, diagnoses and procedures during hospitalization, hospital location, size, ownership and teaching status, clinical outcomes, and total charges. Since October 1, 2015, transition from the International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD‐9‐CM) to Tenth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD‐10‐CM) for hospital discharge data has been implemented for US hospitals. Many studies have reported that the coding transition affected case volume and prevalence estimates. Therefore, we focused on data collected during the ICD‐10 period from NIS 2016 to 2019 to avoid potential bias from the coding transition. The NIS data were de‐identified, and a data user agreement was signed before we analyzed the data. Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project is Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act‐compliant, and therefore review by an institutional review board is not required.
Study Population

A flow chart of the sample selection process is presented in Figure 1. Overall, 158 372 inpatient hospitalizations were identified with a primary diagnosis of PAD using the ICD‐10‐CM codes (Table S1–S7), and PAD‐related procedures were identified using the Procedure Coding Classification System (ICD‐10‐PCS) (Table S2). Missingness occurred in the following variables, including race (Nmissing=3963, 2.5%), estimated neighborhood median household income (Nmissing=2773, 1.75%), patient rural/urban residence (Nmissing=560, 0.35%), elective procedure (Nmissing=498, 0.31%), month when admitted (Nmissing=183, 0.12%), primary payer (N missing=168, 0.11%), death (Nmissing=87, 0.05%), and sex (Nmissing=15, 0.009%). Cases with missing values accounted for 4.7% of the entire data set and were removed from analysis, yielding a remaining sample size of 150 921 for model development and testing. Imputation was not performed in this study because literature has suggested that multiple imputations provide little or negligible benefits (eg, reduce biases and improve efficiencies) as opposed to complete case analysis when there are <5% of missing observations in the data.
Sample selection flow chart.
Data were also split yearly for time‐series cross validation to assess model robustness.
Outcome
The primary outcome was in‐hospital mortality, which is defined as the event of death during hospitalization. The NIS database's death records and diagnosis codes have a high accuracy rate.
Measurement of Predictors

A total of 34 predictor variables were selected based on data availability and findings from prior literature, including patient demographic characteristics, socioeconomic factors, admission characteristics, hospital‐related factors, comorbidities, and surgeries and procedures during the hospitalization (Table 1). These variables have been shown to be associated with higher mortality rates among patients with PAD.

Rural hospitals with bed size between 1 and 49, urban, nonteaching hospitals with bed size between 1 and 99, and urban teaching hospitals with bed size between 1 and 299 were classified as small hospitals; rural hospitals with bed size between 50 and 99, urban nonteaching hospitals with bed size between 100 and 199, and urban teaching hospitals with bed size between 300 and 499 were classified as medium hospitals; and rural hospitals with bed size >100, urban nonteaching hospitals with bed size >200, and urban teaching hospitals with bed size >500 were defined as large hospitals.

Patients' demographic characteristics included age, sex, and race/ethnicity. Patients' socioeconomic factors included health insurance status, rural–urban residence, and neighborhood median household income. Rural–urban residence was measured using the National Center for Health Statistics urban–rural code: 1 “Central” Counties of metro areas of ≥1 million population; 2 “Fringe” Counties of metro areas of ≥1 million population; 3 Counties in metro areas of 250 000 to 999 999 population; 4 Counties in metro areas of 50 000 to 249 999 population; 5 Micropolitan Counties; and 6 Not Metropolitan or Micropolitan Counties. Neighborhood median household income was measured by the estimated median income for patient ZIP code as a proxy for socioeconomic status. The NIS‐constructed neighborhood income variable was categorized into 4 quartiles; the poorest neighborhoods had values less than the first quartiles, and values for the wealthiest neighborhoods were above the third quartile. Patients' health insurance status was measured by the expected primary payer (Medicare, Medicaid, Private insurance, Other insurance, Self‐pay, or No charge) because NIS is a nationwide all‐payer database and thus includes patients with all insurance types.

Admission‐related variables included month when admitted, weekend admission, and emergency department record. We grouped months by season: December, January, February (winter), March, April, May (spring), June, July, August (summer), September, October, and November (autumn) because admission season was shown to be associated with in‐hospital mortality. Weekend admission measured whether patients were admitted to the hospital during weekends and was associated with a higher risk for in‐hospital mortality. Emergency department record indicates evidence of emergency department services reported on the inpatient billing record. Hospital‐related factors were measured by hospital bed size (Small, Medium, and Large), location and teaching status of the hospital (Rural, Urban nonteaching, and Urban teaching), hospital ownership (Public, Private, not‐profit and Private, invest‐own), and census region of the hospital (Northeast, Midwest, South, and West).

Comorbidities included all the conditions in the Carlson Comorbidity Index except for PAD, because all patients in our analytic sample had a primary PAD diagnosis. The 17 conditions (acute myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, PAD, dementia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, rheumatoid disease, peptic ulcer, mild liver disease, diabetes without complications, diabetes with complications, hemiplegia or paraplegia, renal disease, cancer, moderate/severe liver disease, metastatic cancer, and AIDS) in the Carlson Comorbidity Index are strong predictors of in‐hospital mortality and were identified using ICD‐10‐CM codes (Table S3). PAD‐related surgeries and procedures were included: whether patients received elective procedures, whether patients underwent amputation, and whether they underwent endovascular revascularization procedure. We also included the total number of diagnoses and total number of procedures during the hospitalization as predictors.
Data Preprocessing

All categorical variables were coded using the following protocol: ordinal variables were converted to integer values from 1 through k, and nominal variables were encoded using a one‐hot approach, which creates a binary column for each category and returns a sparse matrix. A 5‐fold cross‐validation method was applied to train and test the ML models. Specifically, the dataset was split randomly into a training set (80%) and a test set (20%). This process was repeated 5 times, resulting in 5 distinct test sets. During training, a random selection of 20% data from the training set was used to validate the models. Data were split in a stratified fashion to ensure the same distribution of the outcome classes (with and without mortality) in each subset as the entire set. To further assess model robustness and avoid any potential bias from time‐series data, each model was also trained and tested in a by‐year cross‐validation approach. Specifically, data from each year were used as the test set while the other 3 were used as the training set in each iteration.
ML Models

Four ML algorithms were trained and tested in a binary classification task for in‐hospital mortality, including logistic regression, random forest, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), and light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM). Specifically, a random forest is an ensemble learning method that combines the outputs of many parallel decision trees to improve performance and reduce noise. It is a classic ML model that has been used in a variety of tasks. XGBoost is also an ensemble of decision trees, but it differs from the random forest in that these trees are weak prediction learners and connected in a sequential or gradient boosting fashion. Such structure allows a new learner to concentrate on areas where the existing learners are performing poorly, resulting in less error in the entire model. Compared with the XGBoost, the LightGBM has a similar structure of multiple decision trees connected in a gradient descent fashion, but it uses a different strategy to split the data. Both XGBoost and LightGBM have been shown to outperform random forest in many tasks and represent state‐of‐the‐art ML techniques. Logistic regression served as a baseline model to allow unbiased performance assessment for these ML models.

Grid search was performed to obtain the optimal hyperparameters for each algorithm. The candidates of each hyperparameter were first determined empirically from a plot showing both the training and validation losses against a range of values. The best hyperparameter combinations were achieved through 5‐fold cross‐validated grid‐search with the goal to maximize the average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Each ML algorithm with the best hyperparameters was trained to achieve convergence on the training set. The cutoff threshold of each model was determined at the top left corner of the receiver operating characteristic curve (ie, maximum sum of sensitivity and specificity) from the validation set and applied unchangeably to the test set. All training and testing were done in a Python 3.8 environment using scikit‐learn v1.02, an open‐source package for ML.
Feature Importance

The importance of each predictor variable in a model was assessed by the permutation score on the test set. This score is defined as the decrease in model performance (the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) when all values of a given variable are randomly shuffled. Specifically, this procedure breaks the relationship between the feature and the outcome; therefore, the magnitude of model performance reduction reflects how much the model depends on this particular feature. For each variable in a model, this process was repeated 50 times to obtain an average score.
Statistical Analysis

Descriptive statistics were computed to characterize the baseline features of this data set. The performance of each ML model was assessed by accuracy, recall, specificity, precision, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, and area under the precision‐recall curve. Results were averaged over 5 cross‐validation folds and expressed as mean±SD. All statistical analyses were performed using Python (Version 3.8) and Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA).
Results

In‐hospital mortality occurred in 1.8% (n=2785) of patients hospitalized primarily because of PAD and did not differ meaningfully on a yearly breakdown (Table S4). The mean (SD) age was 67.2 (12.9) years, 39.1% were women, 65.6% were White, and 19.0% were Black patients (Table 1). Nearly 30% of hospitalizations were from large central metropolitan counties, compared with only 8% from nonmetropolitan counties. A higher proportion of patients (36%) live in ZIP‐code areas with the lowest quartile of median household income than those who live in ZIP‐code areas with the highest quartile of median household income. Two‐thirds of hospitalized patients were Medicare beneficiaries, and 54% did not use emergency department services. Among individuals hospitalized with PAD, 53% of patients were admitted to tertiary hospitals, 73.6% were admitted into urban teaching hospitals, and 74.7% were treated in private nonprofit hospitals. Overall, 43.3% of PAD hospitalization records were from the US South. Patients' hospital admissions were highest in spring (25.9%), followed by winter (25.2%), summer (25.1%), and autumn (23.9%), 12.0% of patients were admitted to the hospital during weekends, 37.5% of the patients with PAD received elective procedures, 11.6% underwent amputation surgery, and 53.9% received a revascularization procedure. Most patients had comorbidities, including 74.4% with congestive heart failure, 48.9% with diabetes complications, 38.3% with diabetes only, 33.0% with renal disease, and 24.9% with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

The best hyperparameters and performance outcomes for each model are shown in Table S5 and Table 2, respectively. Overall, each model had comparable performance in predicting inpatient mortality, with a mean accuracy score of 72.0% to 74.8%. In addition, these models yielded an average recall of 77.5% to 82.2%, suggesting their clinical potential for risk stratification. The XGBoost and the LightGBM had the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and area under the precision‐recall curve scores, which reflected marginally better predictability for this task because both metrics were independent of thresholds.

The top 10 critical features predicting mortality in each ML model are shown in Figure 2. The full list of features and their relative importance scores for each model are shown in Table S6. The top 7 critical predictors of mortality were consistent across all 4 models, including the total number of procedures during hospitalization, the total number of diagnoses during hospitalization, age in years, endovascular revascularization procedure, congestive heart failure, diabetes without complications, and diabetes with complications. The 2 gradient‐boosted models also revealed amputation as an important feature for in‐hospital mortality among patients with PAD. The random forest model and the XGBoost selected myocardial infarction and renal disease as ninth and 10th most important predictors. However, sex and race/ethnicity were not revealed by any of the ML models as the top 10 most important features, though they were still among the critical features based on the feature importance scores (Table S6). The time‐series cross‐validation showed almost identical results on both the performance metrics and the critical features for all models (Table S7 and Figure S1).

Discussion

PAD is a major health care problem, and this condition has a high mortality during hospitalization when compared with ischemic stroke. Using the NIS 2016 to 2019, we identified all patients admitted to the hospital primarily because of the PAD diagnosis. ML models were established to predict in‐hospital mortality and reveal important risk factors. Our models suggested that patients who were older, had diabetes, diabetes complications, congestive heart failure, underwent revascularization procedure or multiple procedures, and had multiple diagnoses during hospitalization were at higher risk of dying in the hospital. This is the first study that develops multifactor ML models predicting in‐hospital mortality based on a large inpatient sample of patients with PAD.

ML has been increasingly applied as a robust tool for data‐driven research in medicine. Compared with traditional statistics, ML makes minimal assumptions about the characteristics of data and is effective even when the data are obtained without a carefully controlled experimental design or in the presence of complicated nonlinear interactions. Numerous ML studies based on either the classic (eg, random forest, support vector machine, and k‐nearest neighbors) or the state‐of‐the‐art models (eg, XGBoost and LightGBM) have shown their potential in generating accurate predictions to allow precision medicine. In the current study, a mean sensitivity of ≈80% indicates that each model may adequately identify patients who are at increased risk of in‐hospital mortality. In particular, the 2 gradient boosting models had small improvement in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and the area under the precision‐recall curve scores compared with the parallel trees and the baseline model, further supporting the advantage of this structure. It is noteworthy that the magnitude of performance gain by ML over the traditional regression models might have been limited by a highly imbalanced class distribution (only 1.8% mortalities) of this data set, which has also been observed in previous studies on low‐incidence diseases.

Patients with PAD are increasingly recognized as a group of individuals who are at high risk for poor short‐ and long‐term outcomes. Therefore, validated predictive tools will be highly beneficial in this patient population. In addition, the approach described in our study can be applied to other studies and populations to build, test, and refine predictive models. For example, this could lead to the development of predictive scoring tools such as those used for patients with acute coronary syndromes. Alternatively, validated models can be deployed as a mobile app or integrated into the electronic health record system for real‐time assessment of patient mortality.

Factors linked to poor outcomes must be identified before they can be considered for optimized or focused treatment. Previous studies have consistently reported that patients with PAD with diabetes have higher mortality than those without diabetes. Diabetic foot ulcer predicts a higher risk of amputation and mortality, particularly among those with PAD and advanced age. The presence of lower extremity PAD independently predicts in‐hospital mortality among patients with coronary artery disease or heart failure undergoing coronary artery bypass surgery. However, neither of these studies has reviewed different conditions comprehensively and weighed their importance in predicting adverse clinical outcomes such as mortality. The present study contributes to the current literature by assessing the relative importance of each independent feature and condition in predicting a poor clinical outcome. The top 7 critical features, including age, heart failure, and diabetes, were consistent across 4 models and with prior literature in their associations with mortality. This finding supports the internal consistency of these ML models and indicates that they were not driven by spurious relationships. It also has an important clinical implication. Within a comorbid condition (for example, diabetes), the development of the condition may not be modifiable, but the degree of glycemic control may be better managed during hospitalization to reduce the risk of death. The ML models also suggest that patients with poorer health conditions or undergoing more procedures are more likely to die. Although no causal conclusion can be drawn that more diagnosis or more procedures independently cause increased risk of patient death, this finding still provides valuable information regarding the importance of patient's health condition in relation to other factors. Also, when these 2 features can be estimated for individual patients after hospital admission, the risk of in‐hospital mortality may be predictable.

The present study differed from prior studies in that race/ethnicity and sex were not identified as the most critical predictors of poor outcomes, though they were still associated with in‐hospital mortality. It is likely because previous studies did not assess comprehensively all comorbid conditions along with race and sex information, and the inclusion of big data in our study on comorbid conditions and procedures reduced the previously documented disparities in mortality outcome by race/ethnicity or sex.

This study has several limitations. First, the NIS database contains only hospital‐based discharge data, which provide no follow‐up information for any potential assessment of long‐term outcomes such as hospital readmission or 1‐year mortality rate. Also, we did not assess outcomes other than in‐hospital mortality such as patients discharged to hospice care, length of stay, and total inpatient charges because the current study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of ML models in predicting clinical outcomes. In future research, we will assess other nonclinical outcomes and long‐term outcomes. Second, there is a limited amount of information on patients' socioeconomic characteristics, social determinants, and health behaviors. Several factors that may also be associated with in‐hospital mortality are not available from this database, such as smoking and physical activity. Nevertheless, this limitation is partially addressed by using proxy features such as median household income in patients' residential neighborhoods, rural–urban location, and census region to reflect their socioeconomic status. In addition, there were no pharmacologic data available; therefore, we were not able to include other potential predictors such as antiplatelet therapy and statin therapy. Third, in‐hospital mortalities only occur in a small portion of patients with PAD, resulting in a highly skewed class distribution (98.2: 1.8). An imbalanced data set is commonly seen in ML studies on diseases with low incidence or prevalence rates and is a potential cause for biased models and underestimation of differences in model predictability. Although these concerns were largely alleviated by using stratified cross‐validation and allowing assignment of class weights in this study, the benefit of ML over the baseline model still might not have been faithfully reflected. It further implies that the traditional regression approach, which is simple, explainable, and capable of yielding almost equivalent performance to other complicated ML models, should not be ruled out as an option for risk prediction in low‐incidence diseases. Finally, this study focused on developing and comparing 4 ML algorithms. However, this is a very active area of research in data science. Future work could compare the performance of emerging ML methods with those described in this article.

In conclusion, this study demonstrated the feasibility of using ML models to predict clinical outcomes in patients hospitalized because of PAD. The results will contribute to best guide identifying factors that need to be the focus for personalized intervention.
